rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: The ratio $\\\\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is NOT always 5/3 or 7/5. It depends on temperature and molecular structure. At very high temperatures, vibrational modes activate, changing $\\\\gamma$.  ·  The formula $C_V = \ rac{3}{2}R$ applies ONLY to monatomic ideal gases. For diatomic or polyatomic gases, rotational (and sometimes vibrational) modes contribute.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Dulong's law ($C \\\\approx 3R$) for solids works well at room temperature but fails at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze out degrees of freedom). Einstein and Debye developed low-temperature models.  ·  The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is NOT the same as the gas constant R. $k_B = 1.38 \ imes 10^{-23}$ J/K per molecule. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) per mole. $R = N_A k_B$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution was first derived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1860 and later generalized by Ludwig Boltzmann. It describes the distribution of speeds in an ideal gas and is one of the most important results of kinetic theory.  ·  At 300 K, the three speed measures for nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) are: most probable $v_p \\\\approx 422$ m/s, mean speed $v_{mean} \\\\approx 477$ m/s, and rms speed $v_{rms} \\\\approx 517$ m/s. The ratios are always $v_p : v_{mean} : v_{rms} = \\\\sqrt{2} : \\\\sqrt{8/\\\\pi} : \\\\sqrt{3} \\\\approx 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732$.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Boltzmann constant:** $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \ imes 10^{-23}$ J/K. It connects microscopic and macroscopic thermodynamics. Named after Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906).  ·  **RMS speed:** $v_{rms} = \\\\sqrt{3RT/M}$, where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. At STP (273 K), $v_{rms}$ for air is about 479 m/s. At 300 K, about 484 m/s. Lighter gases move faster on average.  ·  **Most probable speed:** $v_p = \\\\sqrt{2RT/M}$. This is the speed at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks. At 300 K for air: $v_p \\\\approx 364$ m/s. At 300 K for H₂: $v_p \\\\approx 1650$ m/s.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Heat capacities of gases and solids and other topics  ·  Most probable speed is NOT the average speed. For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p \\\\cdot \\\\sqrt{2} < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$. The order is always $v_p < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$ at the same temperature.  ·  Heat capacity is NOT the same as specific heat. Heat capacity $C$ is for the whole object; specific heat $c$ is per unit mass. Molar heat capacity $C_m$ is per mole. They are related: $C = mc$ for uniform objects.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $C_P \neq C_V$. Many students think the heat capacity is the same regardless of conditions. At constant pressure, the gas expands and does work, requiring more heat input to achieve the same temperature rise. $C_P > C_V$ always.  ·  The Dulong-Petit law ($C \approx 3R$) works only at sufficiently high temperatures (well above Debye temperature). Below that, quantum effects dominate and heat capacity drops. For diamond, this 'high temperature' is over 2000 K!  ·  Degrees of freedom 'freeze out' at different temperatures. At room temperature: translational (always active), rotational (active for most molecules), vibrational (usually frozen). The textbook $C_V$ values assume rotational but not vibrational modes are active.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Heat capacity depends on temperature for real substances. The values $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ for diatomic gases are approximate room-temperature values. Over a wide temperature range, $C_V$ can change significantly.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Heat capacities of gases and solids  ·  Note 4: Remember the units and dimensions involved in Heat capacities of gases and solids
